family: recursion on words over two 3-cell tokens (a stack of frames; a halt needs a rare coincidence at the right end)
summary: Decoded completely: a stack machine on words over 110 and 111 that reproduces the run step for step; the conjecture that every such word leads to a word again is false (a 19-token word halts, Lean), the run itself has not halted in 2,097,152 visits (1.3·10<sup>13</sup> steps), and a halt needs a rare coincidence at one of the few visits that reach the right end; open, probably halting far beyond any run.
title: What is known about 1RB1RA_1LC0LF_1RA1LD_1LB1LE_0LC0RD_---0RA
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1RA_1LC0LF_1RA1LD_1LB1LE_0LC0RD_---0RA.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The behaviour is decoded completely: during a visit of the left end the tape is a stack of frames (a block of 1s and a block of 0s each) and a word over the tokens 110 and 111, and twelve transitions on these reproduce the run from blank tape step for step (that the machine follows them is proved in Lean). One of them is the halt. It can only happen in the cascade that follows a visit reaching the right end of the tape, and there it looks like a matter of chance: random words halt at a few in a thousand such visits, and the run has had 31 of them in its first 2,097,152 visits (1.3·1013 steps) without halting. The earlier conjecture that every word over the two tokens leads to such a word again is false: a word of 19 tokens halts (Lean).

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 63,728 cells have been visited and 51,851 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: fixed/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.539). Right of the start it stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half).

claims.title: Shift rules
claims.text: For every length n of the run and any tape around it: L (111110110)^n D> 1 R reaches L D> 1 (101101101)^n R; L (011011111)^n E> 0 R reaches L E> 0 (110110110)^n R; L (110)^n D> 1 R reaches L D> 1 (101)^n R. These are the moves the head makes across the long uniform stretches of the tape.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>11</sup> steps
claims.text: tools/c/tmrun.c runs 1011 steps from blank tape without a halt.

claims.title: The collapses of the block
claims.text: Up to 10<sup>9</sup> steps the periodic block at the left end grows by one copy every three visits and is swallowed thirteen times, with 11, 9, 84, 36, 135, 100, 36, 324, 36, 36, 260, 999 and 36 copies just before; the value 36 recurs five times.

claims.title: The tape is a word over two tokens
claims.text: With b = 110 and c = 111: at each of the 74,198 moments in the first 2·1010 steps when the head stands in B on the blank cell left of the tape, the whole tape is a word over b and c (the longest has 83,005 tokens). The periodic block is a = c b b.

claims.title: A visit is a recursion on the word
claims.text: The next word is b V(X) for w = b X, with V(b X) = c c X, V(c c b c^n b Y) = c b c c b^n V(Y), V(c b c^n b Y) = c b b b^n V(Y). These rules give the next word at 2,239 of 2,361 visits up to 3·107 steps and never a wrong one; at the other 122 the rest starts with c c c, a case not decoded. These are special cases of the stack model below.

claims.title: The complete recursion: a stack model
claims.text: During a visit the tape is a stack of frames 1^n 0^z followed by one of RET(q, v) (the head coming back, 1^(q-1) C>1 and the word v), Z(v) (C on the last zero of the top frame) or CALL(m, X) (1^m B> and the word X); twelve transitions with exact step counts (README, py/model.py). Each time the returning head finds three zeros in the top frame it runs a whole visit on the word to the right: visits inside visits. The model agrees with direct runs of the machine: the next word and the step count of the visit on each of the 131,070 words of at most 16 tokens, and the word and step number of each of the 74,198 visits of the first 2·1010 steps from blank tape (byte-identical output of c/dvis.c and c/wrun.c dump).

claims.title: The machine follows the model
claims.text: The model is a Lean function mstep on states (a list of frames and RET, Z or CALL with a word), and den gives the tape a state stands for. mstep_next: when mstep s is a state s' with a step count k, the machine goes from the tape of s to the tape of s' in exactly k steps. mstep_halt: when mstep s is the halt, the machine halts. mrun_sound, blank_runs_of_mrun: a run of the model from RET(1, c) on the empty stack is a run of the machine from blank tape. Not proved: that the model is never stuck (it is not, in any computation), and that the C and Python programs are the same function as mstep (they count the same steps).

claims.title: 130,661 steps from blank tape through the model
claims.text: 20,000 transitions of the Lean model, run by the kernel, are 130,661 steps of the machine from blank tape without a halt: a check that the whole chain from the model to the machine closes.

claims.title: 33,257,365 steps from blank tape through the model
claims.text: 5,000,000 transitions of the Lean model, evaluated by compiled code, are 33,257,365 steps without a halt; py/model.py counts the same number.

claims.title: Every line of the transition table is a theorem
claims.text: Frames and the two ways a word is written on the tape are defined in Lean, and each transition of the model is proved for the machine at any depth of the stack: the tape of the left-hand side reaches the tape of the right-hand side in the stated number of steps (ret_stride, ret3, ret2, ret2_pop, ret1, ret1_pop, ret1_one, z_call, z_call_end, call_word, call_end, and the versions at the bottom of the stack); ret1_halt: RET(1) on a frame of one 1 and one 0 above a 0 halts; blank_to_model: two steps from blank tape the machine is in RET(1, c) on the empty stack; visit_of_ret1: RET(1, v) on the empty stack is two steps before the head stands in B on a blank cell with blank tape on its left and v on its right.

claims.title: The tape moves of the model
claims.text: Every transition of the model is one of these moves, each proved for every repeat count and any tape around it: the strides of the returning head (stride, stride1, stride_q2), the turns at a frame (ret1_fill, ret1_split), the turn on a zero and the run to the right (z_turn, a_run), the calls (call_cb, call_c; b_eat) and the halt: L 0 1 0 C>1 R halts on its fourth step (halt_pattern).

claims.title: Where the halt sits in the model
claims.text: The machine halts exactly when the head returns in phase (RET(1, v)) to a top frame of one 1 and one 0 (tape 0 1 0 C>1). As long as no call runs off the right end of the word, every frame has a number of zeros that is 2 mod 3 and this cannot happen; the model is then a recursion on words alone, F(c^a b X) = b^(a+1) T(X) for the visit and T(c^j b Y) = c F^j(c Y) for the call (j visits inside the visit). Only a visit that reaches the right end brings frames out of phase.

claims.title: Short words: the first halting ones have 19 tokens
claims.text: The first visit on every word of at most 18 tokens (524,286 words) ends with a word again. Two words of 19 tokens halt, one of 20, five of 21, eleven of 22. Of 20,000 random words of 1,000 tokens, each run for 300 visits, 35 halted, among 20,230 visits that reached the right end; of 3,000 random words of 10,000 tokens, 1,000 visits each, 5 halted, among 1,287.

claims.title: No halt in the first 2,097,152 visits (1.3·10<sup>13</sup> steps)
claims.text: The model run exactly from blank tape, with words and frames run-length coded: visit 2,097,152 is at step 13,274,338,602,371. The right end was reached in 31 visits (the latest: 113,145, 118,809, 231,897, 232,177 and 1,095,353), each followed by a cascade of tens of thousands of out-of-phase transitions; the head came back twelve times to one of seven frames with a single 1, always with 2, 5 or 8 zeros (a halt needs 1).

claims.title: It probably halts, far beyond any run
claims.text: Visits that reach the right end keep coming at about 1.5 per doubling of the number of visits. In the run the returning head met a frame with a single 1 in 4 of the 31 such visits (12 meetings); on random words of 10,000 tokens there are about as many such meetings per right-end visit (583 in 1,287) and one meeting in a hundred is a halt (5 of 583; for words of 1,000 tokens 35 of 2,959). The words of the run look random behind the periodic block (in one long visit the token statistics of 1.4·10<sup>8</sup> calls matched fair coin flips to three digits; the visits inside a visit form a critical branching process). At these rates a right-end visit halts with probability about 0.4%, and a halt becomes likely only around visit 2<sup>150</sup> or later, when the tape would hold about 2<sup>150</sup> tokens. The events of one deterministic run are not independent trials, so this is an estimate only.

claims.title: The halting pattern, and how close the run comes
claims.text: By the transition table the machine halts exactly when C reads a 1 and the three cells to its left are 0 1 0. In 2·1010 steps the run was one cell from this 12,171 times (C reads 1, D reads 0, B reads 1), each time with a 1 in place of the first 0.

claims.title: Words do not always lead to words: a word that halts
claims.text: Started on the visit of the 19-token word b c c c b b b b c c b b b b b b c b c (b = 110, c = 111; head in B on the blank cell left of it) the machine halts on its 6,323rd step, evaluated by Lean's kernel. This refutes the earlier conjecture that every word over b and c leads to such a word again (it had been checked on 81,918 words of at most 16 tokens). The configuration is not one of the run from blank tape.

claims.title: No proof by window automata
claims.text: Finite automata reduction with automata that remember the nearest 6 to 15 cells of one side, the token phase and that the rest is a word over b and c finds no certificate.

claims.title: No halt in the first 2·10<sup>10</sup> steps (second program)
claims.text: An independent direct simulation, which also counts the visits.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>12</sup> steps
claims.text: A direct C simulator on blocks of 16 cells (a full table for every block, state and side of entry; checked against tools/c/tmrun.c: the same number of 1s on the tape after 3·108 steps) runs 1012 steps from blank tape without a halt; the tape then spans about 1.6 million cells.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. In the stack model the halt is one explicit case, a returning head meeting a frame of one 1 and one 0, which can only arise in the cascade after a visit reaches the right end of the tape. No invariant excludes it (words over the two tokens can halt), and a run long enough to see it is out of reach if the estimate of about 2<sup>150</sup> visits is right.

claims.title: Where a halt can come from
claims.text: If the machine halts on its third step from a configuration, that configuration is one of: D with 0 two left, 1 left, 0 under the head. So a run can reach a halt only through one of these patterns, and a proof that the machine never halts only has to rule them out. The proof splits on the state and the five cells around the head.

claims.title: Regular-language deciders tried (F11)
claims.text: None of these closes: each reaches a halting configuration in its abstraction, which says nothing about whether the machine halts. n-gram CPS (tools/c/ngramcps.c), equal widths on both sides: a halting local configuration is reached with plain up to width 20, history 1 up to width 16, history 2 up to width 15, history 3 up to width 14, LRU history up to width 5 (larger widths ran out of the 150 s or 60 million configuration budget). n-gram CPS with every cell tagged by its position mod p: fails for p = 2 up to width 16, p = 3 up to width 16, p = 4 up to width 16, p = 6 up to width 16. n-gram CPS where each side also carries the state of a small automaton that has read that side from the far end (every automaton with up to 3 states on both sides, or 4 states on one side), with position mod 1..4 and widths 4, 6, 8: no closed set without a halt in all 120 parameter sets. Run-length windows (the K nearest runs of equal macro cells on each side, run lengths kept exactly below T and mod M above): fails for all 72 parameter sets (cells of 1 to 4 bits, K = 2, 4, 6, T = 2, 4, M = 1, 2, 4). Two-automaton closed tape language by SAT (a deterministic automaton reading each side inward, n states each, CaDiCaL): no solution for n = 2..8; n = 9 not finished in 150 s.
claims.where: sweeps of 13 November 2026 (family F11); the tagged and run-length deciders are not in the repository yet

claims.text: The same table as 1RB0RF_1LC1RD_1LA1LC_1RA1RE_0RB0LD_---0LC up to renaming and mirroring, started in another state; no common configuration in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps of each.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows, but the reason has changed. The tangle on this machine's tape is fully decoded: a word in two letters, and a stack of bookmarks that makes the head rewrite the word again and again from the inside. Halting turns out to be one unlucky case that can only come up on the rare occasions when the head runs all the way to the right end of the tape.

facts.text: The shortest words on which the machine halts: the conjecture that kept it alive forever is false.
of the real run followed exactly (1.3·10<sup>13</sup> steps): no halt.
The estimated chance of a halt each time a visit reaches the right end; 31 such visits so far.

sections.heading: Bookmarks: visits inside visits
html: Write b for the cells 110 and c for 111. At every visit of the left end the tape is a word in these two letters. What happens during a visit was only partly known. It is this:

The head walks right into the word. A b stops it: the b becomes cc and the head turns back. A block of c's does not: the head wipes the block out (it becomes a row of 0s), leaves a row of 1s in front of it, and walks on. That pair, some 1s, then some 0s, is a frame, a bookmark the head will find on its way back. A block of j letters c, with the b behind it, becomes 3j+2 zeros.

<svg viewBox="0 0 560 96" role="img" aria-label="the tape during a visit: frames, then the head, then the rest of the word" style="width:100%;max-width:560px;height:auto;font:11px var(--mono)"><rect x="8" y="30" width="60" height="22" fill="var(--sunk)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/><text x="38" y="45" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--fg2)">blank</text><rect x="68" y="30" width="46" height="22" fill="var(--ink)"/><text x="91" y="45" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">1111</text><rect x="114" y="30" width="56" height="22" fill="var(--cell0)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/><text x="142" y="45" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--fg)">00000</text><rect x="170" y="30" width="76" height="22" fill="var(--ink)"/><text x="208" y="45" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">1111111</text><rect x="246" y="30" width="30" height="22" fill="var(--cell0)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/><text x="261" y="45" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--fg)">00</text><rect x="276" y="30" width="62" height="22" fill="var(--ink)"/><text x="307" y="45" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">11111</text><path d="M338 22 l6 8 l-12 0 z" fill="var(--head)"/><text x="338" y="16" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--head)">head</text><rect x="338" y="30" width="150" height="22" fill="var(--accent-soft)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/><text x="413" y="45" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--fg)">c b b c c b c …</text><rect x="488" y="30" width="64" height="22" fill="var(--sunk)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/><text x="520" y="45" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--fg2)">blank</text><text x="119" y="72" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--muted)">frame 1</text><text x="223" y="72" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--muted)">frame 2</text><text x="413" y="72" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--muted)">the rest of the word</text><path d="M68 58 h102 M170 58 h106" stroke="var(--line-strong)" fill="none"/></svg>

On the way back the head reaches the zeros of the last frame. Every time it finds three zeros there, it fills them and starts a complete visit on the word to its right, exactly as it does at the left end of the tape. A frame made from j letters c therefore makes j visits inside the visit; when two zeros are left the frame is finished and the head goes on to the frame before it. So a block ccc makes the head rewrite everything behind it three times, and those inner visits meet blocks of their own. The blank tape on the left is simply a frame with endless zeros: that is why the visits never stop.

Counting frames, zeros and letters instead of cells gives a small machine with twelve moves (table in the README) that reproduces the real one exactly: the same word at the same step number at each of the first 74,198 visits, 20 billion steps. It can then be run much further than the real one.

Where the halt is. In this picture the machine halts in exactly one situation: the head comes back to a frame that consists of a single 1 and a single 0. Normally that cannot happen, because every frame starts with 3j+2 zeros and loses three at a time (and has at least four 1s). But when a visit runs off the right end of the word, the head comes back one or two cells out of step, zeros get eaten one or two at a time, and for a while anything goes. Whether the fatal frame turns up is then a matter of the exact numbers.

Not all words are safe. It had been hoped that every word in b and c leads to a word again, which would mean the machine never halts. All words of up to 18 letters do. But bcccbbbbccbbbbbbcbc, 19 letters, halts after 6,323 steps (checked by Lean's kernel). So the alphabet alone does not save the machine.

What the real run does. Its visits have reached the right end 31 times in the first 2,097,152 visits (1.3·1013 steps), ever more rarely: about once or twice each time the number of visits doubles. None of these halted. Random words halt at a few such visits in a thousand, and behind the periodic block the real run's word is statistically indistinguishable from coin flips. If that is a fair guide, the machine does halt in the end, but only after a number of visits with something like fifty digits, and there is no known way to skip ahead: the long visits behave like an avalanche that could stop at any moment (a critical branching process). So the question stays open, with a likely answer nobody can check.

sections.heading: Two letters and a rule that calls itself
html: Write b for the three cells 110 and c for 111. Stop the machine each time the head stands on the blank cell left of the tape (a visit). At every one of the 74,198 visits in the first 20 billion steps the tape is a word in the letters b and c, for example
b cbb cbb bbbbbb cc b c b cc bb c
The block cbb repeated at the left is the periodic block seen before. A visit turns the word into the next one. Take off the first b and call the rest X; the new word is b followed by V(X), where

the rest starts withit becomesand then
bc cthe visit is over
c c b c…c bc b c c b…bthe same rule on what follows
c b c…c bc b b b…bthe same rule on what follows
c c cvisits inside the visit (see the fourth look)
The third line with no c's in the middle reads c b b → c b b: the periodic block lets every visit through unchanged. Behind it the word goes through a cycle of three visits,
bbbbb Y → cc bbbb Y → cb cccc b Y → cbb bbbb V(Y)

which adds one copy of cbb, uses up one b, and gives the rest Y one visit. So the rest of the word is the same machine running three times slower, and inside it another one, nine times slower: counters nested in counters. When a level runs out of b's it meets c c c, and a long visit rewrites the word deep inside. Those are the moments when the periodic block is "eaten".
These three rules are the simplest cases of the full picture above; the hope that every word leads to a word again turned out to be false.

sections.heading: A neat end and a disordered middle
html: Stop the simulator whenever the head reaches a new cell on the left. The tape starts with a long periodic block, the word a = 1^5 0 1^2 0 repeated (at some times instead (1^8 0)^k, another word of nine cells). Each visit adds three cells, one copy of a every three visits, and Lean proves how the head crosses the block in both directions, for every length.

Behind the block the tape is disordered: runs of 1s whose lengths are multiples of 3, separated by 0 and 110. This middle keeps changing and eats the block from the inside. Mostly the block wins and grows, but 14 times in the first 109 steps it was swallowed almost entirely, the last time at step 401,140,791, when at least 749 copies went at once. A halt (state F reading a 0) would have to come out of the middle; nothing about it is understood yet.

sections.heading: The collapses are not random
html: The block of copies of 1^5 0 1^2 0 at the left end grows by one copy every three visits of the head and then disappears at once. Just before each of its thirteen collapses in the first 109 steps it had 11, 9, 84, 36, 135, 100, 36, 324, 36, 36, 260, 999 and 36 copies. Five of them at exactly 36 copies: the collapses are triggered by something regular inside the middle region, a clock that has not been identified yet.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.539). Right of the start it stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half).
After 109 steps the tape spans 63,728 cells (37,689 left of the start, 9,934 right), with a density of 1s of 0.814.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machine below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in the other, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.
